summaries.example: Imagine helping a classmate who dropped their books. Helping may be good because it leads to something else, such as your classmate feeling better. That is value from a result. But some philosophers ask whether feeling good, being safe, or being treated fairly is good in its own right.
summaries.summary: The entry explores two ways of talking about value. Intrinsic value is value something has in itself, or for its own sake. Extrinsic value comes from a relationship to something else, such as being useful, causing a good result, or pointing to something good. Philosophers have proposed many possible intrinsic goods: pleasure, freedom, truth, beauty, friendship, health, virtue, peace, and more. Some focus mainly on pleasure and pain, while others think many different things matter. The entry also explains that philosophers disagree about what carries value and whether values can always be compared or added. A happy experience, a beautiful object, and a fair situation might not fit neatly into one simple measuring system. Some thinkers even question whether intrinsic value is a clear or real feature at all. The main lesson is that saying something is valuable raises several different questions: What is valuable? Why is it valuable? What kind of thing has the value? And how should we compare it with other values?
key_ideas: Philosophers distinguish between things that are good in themselves and things that are good because of what they lead to.
Different philosophers suggest different intrinsic goods, including pleasure, knowledge, beauty, friendship, health, freedom, and justice.
Some philosophers think the value of pleasure and pain is basic. This view is often called hedonism.
It is difficult to decide how to compare different goods or how to add their values together.
Philosophers also disagree about what can have value: an object, a person’s experience, a fact, or a whole situation.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us understand everyday moral questions. When we decide what to do, we often care about results, fairness, happiness, friendship, knowledge, or freedom. Knowing the difference between value in itself and value gained from a connection can help us notice what our reasons really are. It also reminds us that important goods may be hard to measure with one simple score.

important_terms.definition: The kind of value something has because it is good for its own sake, not merely because it leads to another good thing.
Value something gets from its connection to another thing that is valuable.
Something that is good in itself, rather than only useful for getting something else.
A thing that helps bring about another result, such as a tool helping someone finish a job.

questions_to_think_about: Is a favorite toy valuable because of what it helps you do, or because of what it is like and what it means to you?
Can something be useful and also valuable for its own sake?
Are friendship and knowledge valuable in the same way as pleasure?
If two good things are together, is the whole always worth exactly the sum of its parts?

summaries.example: Suppose a city must choose between preserving a beautiful wetland and building a useful road. The wetland might be valuable because it supports wildlife, offers beauty, or has value in its own right. The road might have instrumental value because it helps people reach jobs and services. But the case is not settled by naming these values: one must still ask which entities or states of affairs bear value, whether the goods are comparable, and whether the whole outcome has a value that is merely the sum of its parts.
summaries.summary: The entry examines the philosophical distinction between intrinsic and extrinsic value and shows why the distinction is more complicated than the familiar slogan “valuable in itself” versus “valuable as a means.” Intrinsic value is traditionally understood as a kind of nonderivative moral value, while extrinsic value is derivative from a relation to something else. Yet the entry discusses a major distinction between intrinsic and final value. Final value concerns being valuable as an end or for its own sake; it may depend on extrinsic properties, such as an object’s history, role, or relation to human practices. Thus “intrinsic” and “final” need not mark the same division. The entry surveys proposed intrinsic goods, from pleasure and freedom to knowledge, beauty, virtue, friendship, justice, and aspects of the natural environment. It also surveys competing views about the bearers of value, including properties, states of affairs, facts, objects, and experiences. Further disputes concern the status of value claims, the fitting-attitude analysis, and challenges from noncognitivism, pragmatism, and arguments that “good” is always good in some particular way. Finally, the entry considers value comparison. Betterness may be nontransitive; some goods may be incommensurable; and the value of an organic whole may not equal the sum of its parts. Extrinsic value itself can involve causation, prevention, indication, opportunity, or other relations, so instrumental value is only one variety.
key_ideas: The traditional contrast treats intrinsic value as nonderivative goodness and extrinsic value as goodness derived from a relation to something else.
The entry separates intrinsic value from final value: something may be valued for its own sake because of relational or historical features, not only because of its intrinsic properties.
Proposed bearers of value include properties, states of affairs, facts, objects, experiences, and particular instances of properties; no single account is accepted by all philosophers.
Whether value claims are truth-apt is a separate issue from what intrinsic and extrinsic value mean. Cognitivists and noncognitivists can both address those questions.
Computing overall value is difficult because betterness may be nontransitive, goods may be incomparable, and organic unities may defeat simple addition.
Accounts of extrinsic value need not rely only on means-end causation. A thing can be valuable because it indicates, enables, or is otherwise related to something valuable.
summaries.why_it_matters: The distinction matters because ethical theories often depend on what is taken to be valuable in itself. Consequentialist arguments, for example, assess actions partly by comparing the intrinsic value of their consequences. Questions about responsibility, justice, virtue, and vice can also depend on value judgments. At the same time, the entry warns against treating value as a simple numerical resource. Historical significance, beauty, pleasure, virtue, and justice may interact in ways that resist one scale or straightforward addition. Understanding these distinctions makes moral arguments clearer: it helps identify whether a reason appeals to an end, a means, a relation, a feature, or a non

important_terms.definition: Value understood as nonderivative moral goodness: something is good in its own right rather than because of the value of something else.
Value attributed to something because of its relation to another valuable thing; it is often described as derivative or parasitic on that other value.
Value something has as an end or for its own sake. The entry notes that this may not always be the same as value based on intrinsic properties.
Value something has because it is a means to an end. The entry notes that instrumental value may sometimes be treated as final rather than merely derivative.
The claim that value depends on, or is grounded in, non-evaluative features without being identical to those features.
A whole whose value is not simply the total of the values of its parts; combinations can change the value of what is considered together.
A view that moral value claims do not function as ordinary true-or-false descriptions, though noncognitivists can still discuss intrinsic and extrinsic value.
A relation in which two goods cannot be ranked as better, worse, or equal on a meaningful scale.

questions_to_think_about: If a historical object is valuable because of its history, is that final value, intrinsic value, or both?
Can a value claim be meaningful if it is not a statement that is true or false?
Should pleasure and virtue be placed on one scale, or can one be higher without being measurable in the same units?
Does a valuable whole require valuable parts, or can their arrangement create a new value?
If an action prevents something bad but produces nothing good, is it instrumentally good?

summaries.example: Your school is choosing between two projects. One project buys new sports equipment that students will use every day. Another restores a small garden because students enjoy its beauty and wildlife. The equipment may be good partly because it is useful. The garden might be valuable because of what it gives people, because of its natural life, or because someone thinks beauty is good for its own sake. Philosophers would ask whether these kinds of value can be compared fairly.
summaries.summary: This entry asks what it means for something to have value in itself and how that differs from having value because of something else. Intrinsic value is commonly described as being good for its own sake. Extrinsic value is commonly described as derivative: an object, action, or event is good because it leads to, represents, enables, or is otherwise related to something valuable. Philosophers have offered many candidates for intrinsic value. Some emphasize pleasure and the avoidance of pain; this position is called hedonism. Others include knowledge, beauty, friendship, health, freedom, virtue, fairness, peace, or aspects of nature. The entry does not settle the list. It also examines whether “intrinsic value” and “final value” mean exactly the same thing. Final value concerns being an end or being worth having for its own sake. A rare object, for example, might be valued for its own sake because of its history, even though that history is a relational feature. This suggests that final value need not always be based on intrinsic properties. Other disagreements concern what has value. Some philosophers focus on properties; others on facts, states of affairs, experiences, or concrete objects. The entry then considers whether values can be compared and calculated. Betterness might not always be transitive, some values might be incommensurable, and a whole might have a value not predictable by adding its parts. Extrinsic value also includes more than instrumental value: a thing can be good because it indicates, makes possible, or is connected with something good.
key_ideas: Philosophers have proposed many possible intrinsic goods, including pleasure, truth, knowledge, beauty, friendship, freedom, peace, health, and justice.
Hedonism is the narrower view that pleasure is intrinsically good and pain intrinsically bad, though many philosophers think other things have value too.
The words intrinsic and final can come apart: something may be valued for its own sake because of its history or relationship to people.
Philosophers disagree about whether value belongs to properties, experiences, objects, facts, or states of affairs.
It may be impossible to calculate total value by simply adding up every part, especially when parts form an organic unity.
Extrinsic value is broader than usefulness. Something may be valuable because it signals, enables, prevents, or is connected with something valuable.
summaries.why_it_matters: These ideas appear whenever people argue about what should be done. If consequences matter morally, we need to know which features of those consequences are valuable. Questions about justice, responsibility, virtue, and well-being also involve judgments about what is good or bad. The topic matters because it prevents us from treating every good thing as valuable in exactly the same way. It also shows why moral disagreements can be difficult: people may disagree about the list of goods, the kind of thing that bears value, or whether different goods can be placed on one scale.

important_terms.definition: Value something has in itself or for its own sake, instead of only because it produces another valuable result.
Value something receives because it is connected to, useful for, or evidence of something else that is valuable.
Value something has because it is treated as an end, even if that value depends on relationships or history rather than on inner features.
Value that comes from being a tool or route toward an outcome.
The idea that value depends on non-value features, such as causing pleasure, while remaining different from those features.
A whole whose value may differ from simply adding the values of its separate parts.
A theory saying that value judgments are not ordinary descriptions that are true or false; they may express attitudes or guide action.
A situation in which goods cannot be ranked as better, worse, or equal using a shared scale.

questions_to_think_about: Is a trophy valuable because it is useful, because of what it represents, or for its own sake?
Could two people reasonably disagree about intrinsic value without either simply making a mistake?
Are all good things comparable, or might friendship and freedom resist one shared ranking?
Can a group of ordinary parts make a whole that is much better or worse than their separate values suggest?
Is something still instrumentally good if it prevents a bad outcome but causes no good outcome?
